templates.title: Generative credits used against a monthly allowance, and when each account ran out
templates.subtopic: running totals with an explicit frame, first row past a threshold, as-of joins

sections.scenario: A creative suite's generative features (making or editing an image from a text prompt, for example) cost generative credits. In this exercise every plan comes with a monthly credit allowance, a generation that fails is not charged, and an account keeps generating after it has used its allowance (the overage is reported, not blocked). Account owners and the support team want one report: per account and month, the allowance, what was used, and the exact generation at which the account ran out. All plan names, allowances and rules here are this exercise's, not any real plan's; check current docs.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns account_id, month, allowance, charged_generations, credits_used, ran_out_gen, ran_out_at: one row per account and UTC calendar month with at least one charged generation, ordered by month, account_id. A generation is charged when its status is 'succeeded'; failed generations use no credits. month is the first day of the month (a DATE). allowance is the monthly_credits of the account's plan for that month. charged_generations and credits_used count and sum the charged generations. The account runs out at its first charged generation of the month, in (created_ts, gen_id) order, after which its running total of charged credits for the month is at least the allowance: ran_out_gen is that generation's gen_id and ran_out_at its created_ts, both NULL if the account never reached its allowance that month. {{month_rule}} {{plan_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Reaching the allowance exactly counts as running out. The running total restarts each month. The sample has {{accounts}} accounts and {{generations}} generations.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical plans, allowances, credit costs and accounts. Only generation events and their metadata are used; prompts and images are never part of this report. Real plans can have other rules (rollover, add-on credits, slower generation after the allowance); they are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Failed generations excluded before the running total; a running total per account and UTC month with an explicit ROWS frame and a unique tie-break; inclusive comparison with the allowance; the first qualifying generation by (created_ts, gen_id), not the smallest id; NULLs for accounts that never ran out; no row for months with only failed generations; at Very Hard, the as-of plan from plan_changes (the change exactly at midnight counts, a mid-month change waits for next month, a new account uses its first plan); deterministic order; can discuss live balances and late events.

clarifications.q: The running total reaches the allowance exactly at one generation. Is that the one?
clarifications.a: Yes. At least the allowance is running out.

clarifications.q: Does a failed generation count toward running out?
clarifications.a: No. It is not charged, so it neither adds credits nor can be the generation at which the account ran out.

clarifications.q: An account had only failed generations in a month.
clarifications.a: It has no row for that month.

clarifications.q: Two generations of one account have the same created_ts.
clarifications.a: Order them by gen_id; each adds its own credits to the running total.

clarifications.q: Which month does a generation at 00:00:30 UTC on the 1st belong to?
clarifications.a: The new month. Months are UTC calendar months.

clarifications.q: Does an account that never ran out still get a row?
clarifications.a: Yes, with ran_out_gen and ran_out_at NULL.

hints: Filter to charged generations first, then SUM(credits) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, month ORDER BY created_ts, gen_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
The default frame for a window with ORDER BY is RANGE, which gives tied rows the same running total. Say ROWS and order by a unique key.

The first row at or past the allowance: MIN(created_ts) FILTER (WHERE running >= allowance) gives the time; for the id, aggregate ids in (created_ts, gen_id) order and take the first, or use ROW_NUMBER over the qualifying rows.
For the plan in effect at a month's first instant, a LATERAL subquery over plan_changes with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 is the as-of join.
followups: The support team wants "credits left right now" for one account on every page load. Would you run this query, keep a counter, or both, and how do you keep them consistent?
A failed generation is retried by the app and both attempts are logged, one failed and one succeeded. What could double-charge in your report, and what key would you ask the app to log?

A generation is charged when it succeeds, but its event can arrive hours later from a mobile device. Your report already said the account ran out at a given generation. What do you publish when the late event lands earlier in the month?
Plans can now add credit packs bought mid-month that raise the allowance from the moment of purchase. How does "the moment the account ran out" change, and can an account run out twice in a month?

rules.ask: Two generations share a second. What running total does your window give each of them, and which one does your query say ran out?
Where in your query is a failed generation removed, and could it still be the generation at which the account ran out?
An account upgraded on the 20th. Which allowance does your query use for that month, and which does the rule say?
Are gen_ids in time order? What does MIN(gen_id) return when a later generation has a smaller id?
How does that counter stay correct when a generation's success event arrives late or twice?

templates.title: First-week activation of new users, per app and month
templates.subtopic: cohorts from first events, EXISTS within a half-open window, censored cohorts

sections.scenario: A creative suite's product team tracks one early signal of value: a new user of an app who saves a cloud document within their first week. (A cloud document is a file stored in the vendor's cloud storage rather than only on the device.) They want the share per app and install month. Users reinstall apps and install them on new devices, which must not make them new again. Only events are used: an install and a save, never the document itself.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app, cohort_month, new_users, measurable_users, activated, activation_rate, one row per app and cohort month with at least one new user, ordered by app, cohort_month. A user is a new user of an app at their first install of that app in installs; later installs of the same app (reinstalls, other devices) are not new users and start no new window. cohort_month is the first day of the UTC month of that first install. A new user is activated if they have a save of that app with location = 'cloud' at or after their first install and strictly less than 7 days after it. activated counts measurable activated users, and activation_rate = activated / measurable_users, rounded to 4 decimal places (NULL when measurable_users is 0). The report's as_of is {{as_of}}. {{asof_rule}} {{location_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The window is half-open: a save exactly 7 days after the first install is too late, and a save at the install instant counts. A save in a different app counts only for that app. The sample has {{installs}} install rows and {{saves}} saves.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical apps, users and behaviour. The install log covers every user's full history, so a first install in the data is a real first install. "Saved a cloud document" is this exercise's activation signal, not any product's published metric.
sections.criteria: New users from the first install per user and app; reinstalls ignored; the half-open window from the first install; cloud saves in the same app only; a semi-join (no row multiplication); UTC cohort months; at Very Hard, users whose window has not ended by as_of in new_users only and a NULL rate for a cohort with nobody measurable; correct rounding and order; can discuss truncated history and uncertainty.

clarifications.q: A user installed in September and reinstalled in October. Are they in the October cohort?
clarifications.a: No. They are a September new user only; the reinstall changes nothing.

clarifications.q: That user saved to the cloud two days after the reinstall, three weeks after the first install. Activated?
clarifications.a: No. The window runs from the first install only.

clarifications.q: Is a save exactly 7 days after the first install inside the window?
clarifications.a: No. The window is [first install, first install + 7 days).

clarifications.q: A user saved twice in the first week.
clarifications.a: They count once.

clarifications.q: The user installed two apps.
clarifications.a: They are a new user of each app, each with its own window and its own saves.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of activated over measurable users, half away from zero.

hints: Start from MIN(installed_ts) per (user_id, app): that is the cohort, and it removes reinstalls in one step.
Use EXISTS (or a semi-join) to the saves in the window, so several saves do not multiply rows.
Count with FILTER: all new users, measurable ones, and measurable ones who saved. Divide with NULLIF(…, 0).
followups: The install log only starts on a fixed date, so users who installed earlier look new when they reinstall. How would you detect and exclude them, and what would you tell the team about the first months of the report?
Week-one activation is a ratio of two small numbers for a small app. How would you show its uncertainty instead of a bare percentage?
A user may sign in on a second device before any install is logged there. Which identity do you use for "new user", and what breaks if devices are counted instead of users?
The team wants this daily at hundreds of millions of installs. What would you precompute per user and app, and how do you handle saves that arrive late from offline devices?

rules.ask: A user reinstalls three times in a month. How many new users does your query count for them, and in which cohort?
A save lands exactly 7 days after the install. Does your condition include it, and should it?
A user saved four times in their first week. How many times do they appear before your aggregation, and does your count still say one?
A user installed yesterday and has not saved yet. Why is putting them in the denominator wrong, and what is wrong with leaving out only the ones who did not save?
Why do local saves not count here, and how would you report the users who only ever save locally?

templates.title: Content credentials coverage of exported images
templates.subtopic: one state per entity before a join, GROUPING SETS subtotals, HAVING floors

sections.scenario: Creative apps can attach content credentials to an exported file: provenance metadata, recorded with the asset, that says who or what made it and how it was edited. They describe a history; they are not a guarantee that a file is authentic. A team wants to know how often exported images actually carry them, per app, month and format, because some export paths drop metadata. Each export is logged, and each attempt to embed or remove the credentials is a separate manifest event. Only those events are used, never the image.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app, month, format, image_exports, with_credentials, coverage, ordered by app, month, format. Count only image exports: exports whose normalised format is one of jpeg, png, tiff, webp (other formats, such as pdf and mp4, are left out). month is the first day of the UTC month of exported_ts. For every app and month there is one row per image format and one row with format = 'all' that counts every image export of that app and month. with_credentials counts image exports that carry credentials, and coverage = with_credentials / image_exports, rounded to 4 decimal places. Keep only rows with at least {{min_exports}} image exports; the floor applies to each row on its own, including the 'all' row. {{format_rule}} {{event_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). An export counts once however many manifest events it has. An export with no manifest events does not carry credentials. The sample has {{exports}} exports and {{events}} manifest events.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical apps, exports and rates. Content credentials appear here only as metadata recorded against an export; this report measures whether that metadata was attached, not whether any file is genuine, and it never opens the files.
sections.criteria: Manifest events reduced to one state per export before counting; failed events ignored; image formats normalised (case, jpg as jpeg) and non-images excluded; per-format rows and an 'all' row over every image export; an inclusive floor applied per row; UTC months; at Very Hard, the latest non-failed event decides (embedded then stripped is not covered); correct rounding and order; can discuss regressions, privacy-respecting aggregates and incremental builds.

clarifications.q: Does the 'all' row include formats whose own row is below the floor?
clarifications.a: Yes. It counts every image export of the app and month, then the floor applies to it.

clarifications.q: Is a row with exactly {{min_exports}} image exports kept?
clarifications.a: Yes. The floor is "at least".

clarifications.q: An export has two embedded events (a retry).
clarifications.a: It is one export with credentials.

clarifications.q: An export has only failed events.
clarifications.a: It does not carry credentials. failed events never count.

clarifications.q: How is coverage rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of with_credentials over image_exports, half away from zero.

hints: Reduce manifests to one row per export before joining (for example DISTINCT ON (export_id) over the non-failed events, latest first). A plain join counts an export once per event.
Normalise the format once, in a CTE, and filter on the normalised value.
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((app, month, fmt), (app, month)) gives the per-format rows and the 'all' row in one pass; COALESCE(fmt, 'all') labels it, and HAVING applies the floor to each.
followups: Coverage drops sharply for one export format after an app release. What would you check in the data before reporting it as a regression?
A later edit in another app can remove the credentials from a file that had them. Should that change this export's coverage, or is it a different metric? How would you model both?
The team asks for coverage by user to find who strips metadata. What would you push back on, and what aggregate would answer the product question instead?
At billions of exports a month, manifest events arrive minutes after the export. How would you build this report incrementally so a late event updates only its own app, month and format?

rules.ask: An export has three manifest events. How many times is it counted in image_exports by your query?
Which spellings of jpeg does your query treat as one format, and where does jpg go?
Does your 'all' row count exports from formats below the floor? Which does the rule want?
COUNT(DISTINCT export_id) fixes the total. Does it also fix with_credentials when an export has both an embedded and a failed event?
An export was embedded, stripped, then embedded again. What state does your query give it, and why?

templates.title: Splitting a large PDF into at most k parts
templates.subtopic: greedy feasibility check, monotone predicates

sections.scenario: A PDF service lets users split a very large document (a scanned archive, a catalogue) into smaller files of consecutive pages, for example to stay under an attachment size limit. The user asks for at most k parts; the service should make the largest part as small as possible, and it must say exactly where the parts begin. Only page sizes are used, never page contents.
sections.problem: Implement split_pdf(page_bytes, k, overhead, chapter_starts). page_bytes[i] is the size in bytes of page i + 1. Split the pages into at most k parts of consecutive pages; a part's size is overhead plus the bytes of its pages. Return (largest, starts), where largest is the smallest possible size of the largest part, and starts lists the first page number (1-based) of each part when the document is split from the front with every part taking as many pages as fit within largest. {{overhead_rule}} {{chapter_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 pages; every page is at least 1 byte; 1 ≤ k. Expected: O(n log S), where S is the document's total size. A dynamic programme over every split is O(k·n²) and will not finish.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical page sizes and overhead. A real split also rewrites shared resources and links between pages; here a part's size is exactly as stated.
sections.criteria: Binary search over the part size with an O(n) greedy check; correct bounds (largest page plus overhead); overhead paid by every part; starts from the front-greedy split at the optimum, including fewer than k parts; at Very Hard, chapter starts as forced breaks (page 1 and unsorted lists handled) and None when there are more chapters than parts; O(n log S); can prove the greedy check.

clarifications.q: Must I use exactly k parts?
clarifications.a: No. At most k. starts may have fewer entries.

clarifications.q: There are several splits with the same largest part. Which starts do I return?
clarifications.a: The one from the front where each part takes as many pages as fit within largest. It is unique.

clarifications.q: Is a part exactly largest bytes allowed?
clarifications.a: Yes. Fit means at most largest.

clarifications.q: k is larger than the number of pages.
clarifications.a: Allowed. The largest single page (plus overhead) then decides largest, and small pages still share parts in starts.

clarifications.q: Can a single page be split?
clarifications.a: No. Pages are indivisible.

hints: If parts of size C can be achieved with at most k parts, so can parts of size C + 1. That monotonicity is what you binary-search on.
For a given C, filling each part greedily from the front uses the fewest parts possible. That is an O(n) check.
Bounds: largest is at least overhead + max(page_bytes) and at most overhead + sum(page_bytes).
Once you have largest, run the same greedy fill one more time to produce starts.
followups: Prove that the greedy check uses the fewest parts for a given size limit.
Users want parts that are both small and close to equal in page count. How would you change the objective, and does binary search still apply?
The service streams a 2 GB document whose page sizes are known only as it reads. Can you choose the split in one pass, and what do you give up?
Splitting runs for thousands of users at once. How would you cap the cost of one request, and what would you precompute when a document is uploaded?

rules.ask: How many states and transitions does your DP have for 60 000 pages and k = 40? What property lets you avoid it?
What exactly is monotone in your search, and what are your low and high bounds?
Is total size divided by k a valid answer? Show a document where the best split is far from it.
How does a chapter that must start a part change your feasibility check, and when do you return None?

templates.title: Cloud document sync plan from three hashes
templates.subtopic: three-way comparison against a common base, last-write-wins journals

sections.scenario: A desktop app keeps a folder of cloud documents in sync with cloud storage. Each file is identified by its path and a hash of its contents; the client remembers the hash of each file at the last successful sync (the base). Before syncing it must decide, for every file, what to do: send the local version up, bring the cloud version down, delete one side, report a conflict for the user to resolve, or nothing. The decision is made from hashes alone; contents are never compared or read.
sections.problem:
Implement sync_plan(local, cloud, base). Each argument is a list of (path, content_hash). Return {path: action} for every path that appears in any of the three lists. Let l, c and b be the path's local, cloud and base hash (None where the path does not exist). Apply the first rule that matches:

  1. l == c: 'none' (both sides already agree, including both deleted).
  2. l == b: only the cloud changed: 'delete_local' if c is None, otherwise 'download'.
  3. c == b: only this device changed: 'delete_cloud' if l is None, otherwise 'upload'.
  4. Otherwise both changed, differently: 'conflict'.

{{delete_rule}} {{journal_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 paths per list. Expected: O(n) time. Looking each path up by scanning the other lists is O(n²) and too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical files and hashes. These rules are this exercise's; a real sync engine also handles renames, partial uploads, permissions and retries.
sections.criteria: Three dictionaries and a union of keys; the four rules applied in order with None for missing paths; same edit on both sides is 'none'; new files and deletions on each side; edit/delete conflicts; at Very Hard, the last journal entry wins and a None hash is a deletion; O(n); can discuss renames, clocks and incremental sync.

clarifications.q: The same edit was made on both sides.
clarifications.a: l == c, so 'none': nothing to transfer.

clarifications.q: A new file exists only on this device.
clarifications.a: c and b are both None, so rule 3 gives 'upload'.

clarifications.q: A file was deleted here but edited in the cloud.
clarifications.a: 'conflict': both sides changed, differently.

clarifications.q: Is a path that only appears in base included?
clarifications.a: Yes. Every path in any list is in the result; deleted on both sides gives 'none'.

clarifications.q: Does the order of the result matter?
clarifications.a: No. It is a dictionary.

hints: Build one dictionary per list, path to hash. Then each path's three hashes are O(1) lookups.
The set of paths to decide is the union of the three dictionaries' keys.
Apply the rules in the stated order; None for a missing path makes deletions fall out of the same comparisons.
followups: Show that the four rules never lose data in a two-party sync, and name the one case where 'none' hides that both sides changed.
A file was renamed on this device and edited in the cloud. What do these rules do, and how would you detect the rename from hashes?
Conflicts are resolved by keeping both versions. How would you name the copy so that two devices resolving the same conflict do not create two copies?
A user's library has 2 million files and the client should sync in seconds after waking. What would you send to the server instead of three full lists?

rules.ask: How many comparisons does your lookup do for 100 000 paths, and what structure makes each lookup O(1)?
The rules use hashes and a base, not times. What goes wrong with "newest modification wins" when two devices' clocks disagree?
The same path appears twice in a list. Which entry does your dictionary keep, and is that the one the rules want?
When both sides deleted a file, is that a conflict? Walk through the rules for it.

templates.title: Comparing two saved versions of a cloud document
templates.subtopic: shortest edit script, Myers' greedy diff, output-sensitive complexity

sections.scenario: A cloud document keeps its version history: autosaves, and versions the author names. A "compare versions" view puts two saved versions side by side and marks the paragraphs that were removed and the paragraphs that were added. In this exercise each paragraph is represented by a hash of its content, so the comparison works on short strings and never needs the text itself. Long documents, such as a manual with tens of thousands of paragraphs, usually change in only a few places between two versions, and the view must open quickly for them too.
sections.problem: Implement version_diff(old, new, max_edits=None). old and new are lists of paragraph hashes in document order. An edit deletes one paragraph of old or inserts one paragraph of new; there is no "change" operation, so a rewritten paragraph is one deletion and one insertion, and so is a moved one. Return (deleted, inserted) for an edit script with the fewest edits in total. That pair is the same for every shortest script: deleted = len(old) − k and inserted = len(new) − k, where k is the length of a longest common subsequence. {{dup_rule}} {{cap_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 30 000 paragraphs in each version. Two versions usually differ by at most a few hundred edits, spread through the document, not only at its start or end. Something close to O((n + m) · D) is expected, where D is the number of edits. A full n × m table is 9 × 10⁸ cells at this size, too slow and too large.
sections.assumptions: Document sizes and edit counts are hypothetical. Equal hashes mean equal paragraphs; in this exercise there are no collisions. The hash strings are opaque: compare them only for equality.
sections.criteria: Correct (deleted, inserted) with moves and rewrites counted as a deletion and an insertion; correct on empty versions and on repeated hashes; None exactly when the edits exceed max_edits; an algorithm whose cost grows with the number of edits (Myers' furthest-reaching paths, or an equivalent output-sensitive method) with a clear complexity argument; awareness of memory as well as time; sensible answers on recovering the script, moves and merges.

clarifications.q: Is a paragraph that moved one edit or two?
clarifications.a: Two: one deletion where it was and one insertion where it is now. Detecting moves is a follow-up.

clarifications.q: Do I return the edit script itself?
clarifications.a: No, only (deleted, inserted). That pair is unique even when several shortest scripts exist.

clarifications.q: Can the same hash appear twice in one version?
clarifications.a: It depends on the replay. When it can, every empty paragraph has the same hash, and a repeated heading has one hash too.

clarifications.q: What if one version is empty?
clarifications.a: Then every paragraph of the other version is an edit: (len(old), 0) or (0, len(new)).

clarifications.q: What does max_edits mean?
clarifications.a: A cap on the work. If the fewest edits needed is greater than it, return None. When it is None there is no cap.

hints: Draw the edit graph: x moves along old, y along new. A step right is a deletion, a step down an insertion, and a diagonal step, where the paragraphs are equal, is free.
For each number of edits d, keep only the furthest point you can reach on every diagonal k = x − y. A path with d edits ends on a diagonal between −d and d with the same parity as d.
After each edit, follow the free diagonal steps as far as they go. Stop as soon as a path reaches the end of both versions. That d is the answer, and with a cap you may stop early.
followups: The view must show which paragraphs changed, not just how many. How do you recover the edit script without keeping every round's furthest points in memory?
Authors complain that a moved section shows as a long deletion and a long insertion. How would you detect moves, and what would you show?
Within a changed paragraph, the view should highlight the words that changed. What do you run at that level, and how do you stop it being slow on a paragraph that was entirely rewritten?
Two people edited the same base version on different devices. How would you use two diffs against the base to merge them, and where do you need the author to decide?

rules.ask: SequenceMatcher looks for long matching blocks and is not guaranteed to find the fewest edits. Give an input where its edit count is higher than the minimum, or explain how you would test for one.
How many cells is that table for two 30 000-paragraph versions, and how much memory and time would it take in Python?
Why is it enough to keep only the furthest-reaching point on each diagonal? What would go wrong if you kept a point that is not the furthest?
Trimming the common start and end helps when edits are clustered. What does it save when the edits are spread through the whole document?
Two different paragraphs get the same hash. What does the view show, and how likely is that with the hash length you would choose?

templates.title: Breaking a paragraph into lines with even spacing
templates.subtopic: optimal line breaking, bounded inner loops, tie rules

sections.scenario: Layout and document apps set paragraphs of text in columns. Filling each line with as many words as fit, then moving on, can leave one line nearly empty in the middle of a paragraph, which looks like a hole in justified text. Typesetting systems instead choose all the break points of a paragraph together, so that the white space is spread evenly. In this exercise the layout engine gives you the width of every word, and you must choose the line breaks for paragraphs of any length, including very long ones in a large document.
sections.problem: Implement break_lines(widths, line_width, space, forced). widths are the word widths in layout units, in reading order. A line holding words i..j is widths[i] + … + widths[j] + space · (j − i) units wide, and it must be at most line_width. Its slack is line_width minus that width. The cost of a layout is the sum of the squared slack of every line except the last, which is free. Return (cost, starts) for a layout with the least cost, where starts lists the index of the first word of every line. If several layouts have the least cost, return the one whose starts list is smaller, compared element by element as Python compares lists. An empty paragraph returns (0, []). {{width_rule}} {{forced_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 80 000 words in one call. Every width is a positive integer, space is at least 1, and a line holds a few dozen words at most. Something close to O(n · w) is expected, where w is the most words that fit on one line. Trying every later word as the end of each line is O(n²) and too slow.
sections.assumptions: Widths, line widths and spaces are hypothetical whole layout units. Hyphenation, kerning and stretchable spaces are outside this exercise. Squared slack is this exercise's cost rule; production typesetters use richer rules.
sections.criteria: Correct cost with the last line free; correct width arithmetic with spaces between words only; the tie rule implemented and justified; None and (0, []) where specified; forced breaks handled where they apply; a DP whose inner loop stops at the line width, with a clear O(n · w) argument; no recursion-depth hazard; sensible answers on incremental relayout, hyphenation and richer cost rules.

clarifications.q: Does the last line count?
clarifications.a: No. The last line is free, whatever its slack, but it must still fit.

clarifications.q: Is a line that fills the width exactly allowed?
clarifications.a: Yes. Its slack is 0.

clarifications.q: Which layout do I return when two cost the same?
clarifications.a: The one with the smaller starts list, compared element by element. For example [0, 3, 7] comes before [0, 4, 6].

clarifications.q: Can a line hold one word?
clarifications.a: Yes. A single word that fits is always a legal line.

clarifications.q: Are the widths sorted or bounded?
clarifications.a: Neither, beyond being positive integers. A word can be as wide as the whole line.

hints: Let best[i] be the least cost to lay out words i to the end. The line that starts at word i ends at some word j, and the rest is best[j + 1].
Grow the line from word i one word at a time, keeping a running width. As soon as it no longer fits, no longer line fits either, so stop.
Fill best from the end of the paragraph backwards, and on a tie keep the earlier break. Then the starts list you read off from the front is the smallest one.
followups: Typesetters also penalise a tight line next to a loose one. What does that add to your state, and what does it cost?
A paragraph is edited in the middle of a 300-page document. Which lines do you need to recompute, and how do you know when the new layout has rejoined the old one?
Words may be hyphenated at known points for a fixed penalty. How do you add that to the DP?

The inner loop is bounded by the words per line. For very narrow columns that is small, but for very wide ones it is not. What property of the cost lets an algorithm such as SMAWK do better, and does squared slack have it?

rules.ask: Give a paragraph where filling each line as far as it goes costs more than the best layout. What does squared slack punish that greedy ignores?
How deep does your recursion go on an 80 000-word paragraph, and what happens at Python's default recursion limit?
Prefix sums give each line's width in O(1). Does your loop over line ends still stop early, or does it try every later word?
Your costs are integers. Where could a float enter the answer, and what would the output then look like?
Why does keeping the earlier break, when filling the table from the end, give the smallest starts list overall?

templates.title: Debug the monthly font usage report
templates.subtopic: time zones, distinct counts at the right grain, event-type filters

sections.scenario: A font service lets subscribers activate fonts for their desktop apps and add fonts to web projects that serve them on websites. Type designers and the font team read a monthly usage report per font family. The report has drawn complaints. Families with variable fonts appear to have hundreds of styles. A family's desktop account count is higher than the number of accounts that used it. Desktop activations jump in months with large web launches. Users who switched a font off are counted as using it. Activations from the last evening of a month in the Americas appear in the wrong month. The function below produces the report and is the suspect. The report reads only usage events: font, account, surface, project and time, never any document or web page.
sections.problem:
Fix font_usage_report(events) so that it meets this specification. Each event is a dict {"type", "surface", "account", "project", "font", "ts"}, in any order. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Events. type is "activate" or "deactivate". surface is "desktop" (a font activated for desktop apps, project is None) or "web" (a font added to a web project, named by project). Only activate events are counted anywhere. A deactivation never adds to a count and never creates a row.
  2. Fonts. font is "Family/Style", for example "Harbor Serif/Bold Italic". A variable-font instance carries its axis settings after @, for example "Lumen Sans/Roman@wght=650,wdth=85". It is an instance of the style before the @ ("Roman"), not a style of its own.
  3. Months. ts is ISO 8601 with a UTC offset, for example "2026-04-30T21:15:00-05:00". An event belongs to the UTC calendar month of its instant (that example is in "2026-05").
  4. Output. {month: {family: {"desktop_activations", "desktop_accounts", "styles", "web_projects"}}}, with a row for every month and family that has at least one activate event. desktop_activations counts desktop activate events. desktop_accounts counts distinct accounts with a desktop activation of any style of the family. styles counts distinct styles activated on either surface. web_projects counts distinct web projects the family was added to.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name and output format. Up to 200 000 events, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Event names, families, accounts and projects are fictional, and the counting rules are this exercise's rules, not any product's published definitions. Each event is delivered once.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with the complaint it causes; months from the UTC instant; variable-font instances reduced to their style; accounts distinct per family; desktop counters limited to desktop events; deactivations ignored, including for row creation; minimal, linear fixes; a test per bug; sound answers on active-state counts, late events and approximate counts.

clarifications.q: Does a web-project addition count as a desktop activation?
clarifications.a: No. Web additions count only towards web_projects and styles.

clarifications.q: An account activates Regular and Bold of one family. How many desktop accounts is that?
clarifications.a: One. Accounts are counted per family.

clarifications.q: What about activating the same style twice in a month?
clarifications.a: Two activations, one account, one style.

clarifications.q: Which month is "2026-06-01T03:00:00+05:30" in?
clarifications.a: May: that instant is 21:30 UTC on 31 May.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Take one event at a time and write down the month, family and style the code derives from it. Try an evening in UTC−05:00 on the last day of a month.
Which field identifies a style? Look at what the code does with everything after the slash.
For each counter, ask which event types and which surfaces may change it, and at what grain it is distinct.
followups: Font designers want the number of accounts that had a family active at any point in the month, not just those who activated it during the month. What state do you need, and where does it come from?
The report runs daily over the month so far, and events arrive up to two days late. How do you make re-runs give the same answer and handle the late events?
Distinct accounts per family per month over billions of events is expensive. Where would an approximate distinct count be acceptable, and where not?
A family is renamed by its foundry halfway through the month. How do you report it, and what do you keep so last year's reports can still be explained?

rules.ask: The string's date is the local date. Which events end up in the wrong month, and how many hours of each month can that affect?
The report is in UTC months. A designer in Tokyo reads it. Is that the right choice for them, and what would you show instead?
A designer asks how many instances of the variable style were used. Where would you keep that, now that styles collapses them?
Which of these four counters could be approximate, and which must be exact for the people who read the report?
Which single test would have caught each bug, and how would you keep it from passing by accident?

templates.title: Ingesting stock contributions from upload to search
templates.subtopic: review workflows, state machines, search indexing freshness

sections.scenario: A stock content marketplace accepts photos, illustrations, vectors and videos from {{contributors}} contributors and licenses them to customers. About {{daily_uploads}} files are uploaded a day. Each file goes through automated checks and a review before it can be sold, and contributors add a title, keywords and release documents for people or property shown. Contributors are promised a review decision within {{review_target}}. Once an asset is approved it must be findable in search within {{freshness}}, and once it is withdrawn or taken down it must leave search just as quickly.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from upload to search. Cover how uploads land and are identified, the states an asset moves through (uploaded, checks passed or failed, submitted, in review, approved, rejected with a reason, withdrawn, taken down) and how transitions are recorded, the automated checks and how their results are stored, keywords and titles and the edits contributors make after approval, licence types and release documents, how the search index is kept fresh, and the data contributors and the review team see: queue sizes, decision times and rejection reasons.
sections.constraints: A file can be uploaded twice, by the same contributor or another one. Contributors edit keywords after approval, and edits must reach search. A takedown must remove an asset from search and from new licensing within {{freshness}}, even while other updates are queued. Already-licensed copies keep their licence. Reviews are done by people working through queues, and the review target is measured per asset.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, targets and states are hypothetical; licence and review rules are this exercise's rules, not a statement of any marketplace's policy. You may use common building blocks: object storage, a queue or log, a relational store, a stream processor and a search engine.
sections.criteria: Immutable landing with content hashes and upload identity; an explicit asset state machine with append-only transitions and reasons; checks and reviews recorded as results tied to asset and metadata versions; metadata edits versioned and propagated; the search index treated as a rebuildable projection with a freshness target and monitoring; takedowns that cannot be overtaken by stale updates; licences already sold unaffected; queue and decision-time metrics per asset; credible answers on duplicates and reindexing.

clarifications.q: What identifies an asset: the file or the submission?
clarifications.a: You decide, but a contributor can upload the same file twice and two contributors can upload visually identical files. Say how you detect and treat both.

clarifications.q: Can an approved asset change?
clarifications.a: Its title, keywords and categories can be edited. A new file is a new asset.

clarifications.q: Who needs the review data?
clarifications.a: The review team needs queue sizes, ages and decision times; contributors need their own assets' states and rejection reasons.

clarifications.q: How fast must a takedown take effect?
clarifications.a: Within {{freshness}} for search and new licences, and you must be able to prove when it happened.

clarifications.q: Do automated checks decide on their own?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, technical checks (format, resolution, corrupt files) can reject on their own. Anything else goes to human review.

hints: Model the asset as a state machine and store every transition as an append-only event with who, when and why. Current state is derived from it.
Separate the search index from the source of truth: the index is a projection that can always be rebuilt from the asset table and its events.
Give takedowns their own fast path into the index, or a version check that lets them overtake slower updates.
followups: A contributor edits keywords on an asset while a takedown for it is still in flight. Walk through what each system sees, and how you guarantee the takedown wins.
The review queue grows faster than reviewers can clear it, and the {{review_target}} target is missed for a week. What data shows why, and what would you change?
The search index must be rebuilt from scratch after a mapping change. How do you do that without serving stale or missing assets meanwhile?
How would you detect that a newly uploaded file is a near-duplicate of an existing approved asset from another contributor, and what happens next?

rules.ask: A contributor disputes a rejection from three weeks ago. With your model, how do you show who decided, when, and on which version of the metadata?
The index and the asset table disagree for one asset. Which one wins, and how do you find all such disagreements?
What ordering do you rely on between a keyword edit and a takedown for the same asset, and where could that order be lost?
Two contributors upload visually identical files. Who keeps the asset, who decides, and what does the second contributor see?
A takedown must leave search within {{freshness}}. How does a scheduled job meet that?

templates.title: Collecting page views and events from customers' websites
templates.subtopic: beacon collection, sessionisation, bot filtering, late hits

sections.scenario: A web analytics product lets {{customers}} customer organisations put a tag on their websites and apps. The tag sends a hit for every page view and for events the customer defines, such as a sign-up or a video start. Together they send about {{daily_hits}} hits a day. Customers expect today's numbers in their reports within {{report_latency}}, and they expect yesterday's numbers to stop changing. Mobile apps batch hits while offline and can send them up to {{late_window}} later. Bots and monitoring tools also load customers' pages.
sections.problem: Design the collection pipeline from the tag to report-ready data. Cover the collection endpoint and what a hit carries, how a hit is made safe to retry, the buffer and how it is partitioned, validation and enrichment (device and geography from the request, the customer's own processing rules), how visitors and visits are identified and how visits are cut, bot filtering and how its decisions are recorded, hits that arrive late or out of order, what reports read, and the metrics that show the pipeline is complete.
sections.constraints: One customer's data never mixes with another's. A customer's traffic can spike ten times during a campaign. Visitors' consent choices on a site are honoured: hits a visitor did not consent to are not stored. The IP address is used for enrichment and then discarded or truncated. Hits from offline apps arrive up to {{late_window}} late. Any day must be re-processable from raw hits. Restating months of history after a rule change is out of scope here.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and targets are hypothetical; visit and bot rules are this exercise's rules. Each hit carries the customer's tag id, a visitor identifier from the tag, a timestamp from the device, a sequence number within the visit, the page or event, and any consent flags the site set.
sections.criteria: A lean collection endpoint that acknowledges after a durable write; hit identity and deduplication beyond the edge; partitioning with per-customer isolation and a plan for hot customers; consent honoured before storage and IP addresses discarded after enrichment; visits cut by a clear rule with late hits handled; bot filtering recorded, reversible and measured; raw, real-time and finished layers with explicit re-runs; completeness metrics a customer can trust; credible answers on campaign spikes, late batches and new bot rules.

clarifications.q: Which time counts, the device's or the server's?
clarifications.a: Reports use the hit's own time, but device clocks can be wrong. Record both and say how you reconcile them.

clarifications.q: What ends a visit?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, 30 minutes without a hit, or the end of the day in the customer's report time zone.

clarifications.q: How are bots identified?
clarifications.a: From known bot user agents and lists you are given, plus behaviour rules you design. Filtered hits are kept apart, not deleted.

clarifications.q: Can a customer change processing rules?
clarifications.a: Yes, but in this question a rule change applies from the moment it is made. Restating history is a separate problem.

clarifications.q: How late is too late?
clarifications.a: A hit older than {{late_window}} is stored but not added to finished days.

hints: Give every hit an identity from the tag (visitor, visit and sequence number) so a retried request can be recognised later, not just at the edge.
Partition by customer for isolation, but think about what one customer's campaign does to its partitions.
Keep raw, real-time and finished views separate: real-time numbers can be approximate and revised; a finished day changes only through an explicit, logged re-run.
followups: A customer's campaign sends ten times their usual traffic for two hours. What happens at each stage, and what do other customers notice?
An app releases a batch of hits {{late_window}} late, after the day was finished. Where do they go, what do reports show, and what does the customer see changing?
A new bot rule would remove 8% of one customer's page views. How do you test it, roll it out and explain it to the customer?
How do you show a customer that every hit their site sent was received and processed, or how many were not?

rules.ask: You partition by customer. One customer's campaign makes one partition ten times hotter. What changes in your key or your consumers?
A visitor clears cookies and blocks third-party storage. What does your visitor count do, and how do you explain that to the customer?
A monitoring tool uses a normal browser's user agent. What behaviour rule would catch it, and how would you measure the rule's mistakes?
Your watermark closes the day after {{late_window}}. What do customers see in today's real-time numbers when a large late batch arrives?
How long do you remember hit identities, and what does that window cost at {{daily_hits}} a day?

templates.title: Cloud documents as data — versions, named versions, sharing, comments and the document on a date
templates.subtopic: immutable version lineage, restores, effective-dated access grants, comments anchored to versions

sections.scenario: Creative apps on desktop, tablet and phone save design files as cloud documents; about {{documents}} of them exist. While a document is being edited the app autosaves a new version about every {{autosave_minutes}} minutes; a user can also save a version by hand and give any version a name. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), named versions are kept for as long as the document exists and unnamed versions are deleted after {{unnamed_retention_days}} days. A user can restore an older version, which becomes the newest version without deleting anything after it. The owner can share a document with up to {{collaborators}} people as viewer, commenter or editor, or turn on a link that anyone with it can open; access can be changed or revoked at any time. Collaborators leave comments pinned to a spot on the canvas of a particular version, reply to them and resolve them. Product analytics, support and the owners' own "version history" panel all read from your model, and analytics never reads what is inside a document: only ids, sizes, counts, timestamps and the app that saved it.
sections.problem: Design the data model for cloud documents and their history. Cover: documents, versions (keys, lineage, kind: autosave, manual, restore), names on versions, the pointer to the current version, retention and what a deleted unnamed version leaves behind; sharing grants with roles and link sharing, kept so that "who could open this document on a given date" is answerable; comments and replies anchored to a version, and what happens to them when the version they point at is deleted or the document is restored. Then show how to answer "what did this document look like, and who could edit it, on 1 March", and the analytics facts that answer "versions per active document per day by app", "share of documents shared outside the owner's organisation", and "median time from a comment to its resolution".
sections.constraints: A saved version never changes. A restore never deletes or rewrites newer versions. Access history must be reconstructable for any past instant, for support and for audits. Document contents (layers, text, images, file names chosen by the user) never enter analytics tables; component sizes and counts may. Deleting unnamed versions under the retention rule must never break a comment, a name or a restore.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, intervals, retention and collaborator limits are hypothetical. A document has one owner, who may belong to an organisation account. Version contents are stored elsewhere as files referenced by an id; this question is about the metadata that describes them. Clocks on devices drift, but every version gets a server commit time when it is accepted.
sections.criteria: Versions as an immutable, append-only lineage with based-on and restored-from references; current version derived from commit time; names as their own history; retention removing contents while keeping a tombstone row; effective-dated grants for people and links; comments anchored to a version and region with a defined carry-forward rule; the as-of queries for content and access; analytics facts at stated grains with no contents; each incident traced, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do two devices editing at once create branches?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. The service accepts versions one at a time per document; a save based on an older version is still appended, and the app records which version it was based on.

clarifications.q: Does "the document on 1 March" mean the latest version committed by then?
clarifications.a: Yes: the newest version whose server commit time is at or before that instant, which may be a restore of something older.

clarifications.q: Is a link share a grant to a person?
clarifications.a: No. It is a grant to anyone with the link, with its own role, and it can be turned off and on again. Model it so that both kinds appear in "who could open it".

clarifications.q: Can a comment be moved to a newer version?
clarifications.a: The app shows comments from earlier versions on the current one when the spot still exists. You decide how the anchor is stored.

clarifications.q: Does a renamed version keep its old name anywhere?
clarifications.a: Support wants the history of names, yes.

hints: Treat versions as an append-only lineage: each row points to the version it was based on and, for a restore, the version it restored. "Current" is derived from commit time, never a mutable flag you trust alone.
Sharing is a set of effective-dated grants (valid_from, valid_to) per principal and role, including a link principal; "who could open it at time t" is an interval query.
Retention deletes the stored contents of an unnamed version; the metadata row can stay as a tombstone so that names, comments and lineage still resolve.
followups: Write the query (in words or SQL) for "the version current at instant t" and "everyone who could edit at t", including a link share that was on at t.
A comment was pinned to a version that retention has now deleted. What does the comment's row point to, and what does the history panel show?

With autosave every {{autosave_minutes}} minutes, estimate version rows per day across {{documents}} documents if 3% are edited daily for two hours. Which facts do you keep at version grain, and which are daily aggregates?
The owner moves the document to another person who is outside their organisation. Which rows change, which stay, and how does "shared outside the organisation" change for past months?
An audit asks for every person who could open a document over the past year, including through links shared onward. What can and can't your model prove?

rules.ask: A restore and an autosave are accepted within the same second from two devices. How does a flag stay right, and how do you answer "current on 1 March" after it has been flipped many times since?
An editor was downgraded to viewer last week. Support asks whether that person could edit on the day a layer disappeared. How does your model answer?
A comment, a version name and a restore all point at a version that retention removes. What exactly is deleted, and what row is left for them to point at?
The anchored spot no longer exists in the current version. Where does the comment live, and how is "time to resolution" measured for it?
A link was turned off and on again, and someone opened the document in between from an old browser tab. What did your grants record, and what does access history show?

incidents: The retention job deleted unnamed versions older than {{unnamed_retention_days}} days by removing their metadata rows. Comments pinned to those versions disappear from the history panel, and restores of a later version fail because its base version is missing.

An app release autosaves every few seconds instead of every {{autosave_minutes}} minutes for documents left open. Version rows per document jump fifty-fold in a day and the "versions per active document" metric moves with them.

Sharing changes were applied by updating or deleting grant rows in place. On a document shared with {{collaborators}} people, a removed collaborator's row was deleted, and an audit for the previous quarter shows the document as never shared with that person.

templates.title: E-signature agreements as data — participants, signing order, delegation, reminders and audit events
templates.subtopic: participant sets and order, delegation lineage, append-only audit events, content-free analytics

sections.scenario: Business customers send documents for e-signature: about {{agreements_per_month}} agreements a month. A sender builds an agreement from one or more documents or from a saved template, adds up to {{max_participants}} participants with roles (signer, approver, form filler, or cc who only receives a copy), and sets the order: everyone at once, one after another, or groups that go in order while the members of a group act in any order. A participant can delegate their part to someone else, who can delegate again; a participant can decline, which ends the agreement. Reminders go to whoever is currently expected to act every {{reminder_days}} days until they act. An agreement can be cancelled by the sender or expire on a date. For every agreement the service keeps an audit trail of what happened and when, which customers download as evidence and which is kept for {{audit_retention_years}} years under this exercise's rule. Customers' administrators want reports: time to complete by template and sending team, where agreements stall, how often people delegate, and whether reminders help.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: agreements, their documents (as references only) and the template version they came from; participant sets (groups) with their order and the participants in each, with roles; delegation as a lineage that keeps who was originally asked; reminders; and the agreement's lifecycle (draft, sent, in progress, completed, declined, cancelled, expired). Define the append-only event record that is the source for both the customer's audit trail and analytics, and draw the line between the two: what the audit trail must hold that analytics must not. Then design the analytics facts that answer the four reports above, and show how to reconstruct "which participants an agreement was waiting on at 09:00 last Tuesday".
sections.constraints: Document contents, form-field values and signature images never enter analytics, logs or this event record's analytics copy; events carry ids, types, roles, statuses, timestamps, page counts and sizes. Audit events are append-only and must be shown in their true order, with nothing missing. Analytics identifies participants only by pseudonymous ids. An agreement's state at any past instant must be reconstructable. Customers see only their own agreements.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, limits, reminder intervals and retention are hypothetical; they are this exercise's rules (check current docs). Templates are versioned: editing a template never changes agreements already sent from it. Email addresses are needed to deliver an agreement and are kept by the operational service, not by analytics.
sections.criteria: The plan (participant sets, order, roles) frozen at send and separate from events; delegation as lineage keeping the original participant; an append-only event record with a classified, allowlisted analytics projection and no contents or field values; lifecycle states derived from events; as-of reconstruction of who an agreement waits on; facts at stated grains (agreement accumulating snapshot, participant-slot facts) with template version pinned; audit retention apart from analytics retention; each incident contained, purged where needed, and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a delegate replace the original participant?
clarifications.a: The delegate acts in their place, but the record must keep who was originally asked and the chain of delegation.

clarifications.q: Can a group mix roles?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example two approvers and a signer. The group is complete when every member has acted.

clarifications.q: Who receives a reminder after a delegation?
clarifications.a: The current holder, never the original participant.

clarifications.q: What does "time to complete" start from?
clarifications.a: Your choice, stated: sent time is the usual start. Say how you treat agreements that never complete.

clarifications.q: May analytics keep email domains to group participants by company?
clarifications.a: Only if you can justify it as non-identifying; many customers will object. Propose an alternative.

hints: Separate the plan (participant sets, order, roles, as sent) from what happened (events). The plan is frozen when the agreement is sent; each event refers to a participant slot in the plan.
Delegation creates a new holder for the same slot. Store it as an event with from and to, so the original participant and the chain survive.
One event stream can feed both the audit trail and analytics if fields are classified at the source: analytics receives an allowlisted projection, never the raw event.
followups: Write the reconstruction of "waiting on" at a past instant for an agreement with groups that go in order. What do you read, and in what order?
Define "stall": which step, measured from when, and how do delegations and reminders appear on the report?
A template was edited while 40,000 agreements created from it were in flight. Which version does each report attribute them to?

A customer's auditor asks for the full trail of one agreement from {{audit_retention_years}} years ago, while analytics only keeps 2 years of events. Which store answers, and how do you prove it is complete and in order?
At {{agreements_per_month}} agreements a month and up to {{max_participants}} participants each, which facts do you keep at participant-slot grain, and which at agreement grain?

rules.ask: An agreement has twelve participants in four groups, with two delegations. What does your wide row look like, and how do you query "stalled at the third group"?
Which participants was this agreement waiting on last Tuesday at 09:00? Show what your model reads to answer it.
Your analytics table now holds email addresses. Which report needs them, and how would you serve that report without them?
A delegate delegates again and then the second delegate declines. Who declined, in the customer's report and in the audit trail?
How do you measure whether a reminder helped? What is the comparison, and what confounds it?

incidents: A new form-field type started copying the filled value into the event payload. For three days, values typed by signers reached the analytics warehouse for agreements across many customers.

The reminder scheduler ran twice after a failover, so participants received two reminders every {{reminder_days}} days for a week; the "reminders sent per completed agreement" metric doubled and some customers asked whether their signers were spammed.

Stall reports joined agreements to the current version of their template. After a large customer reordered a template's groups, last quarter's report shows agreements stalling at steps they never had.

templates.title: Content credentials as data — provenance manifests, actions, ingredients and verification results
templates.subtopic: provenance manifests as a DAG, hash binding, recorded actions, verification as observations

sections.scenario: Creative apps can attach content credentials when an image is exported: a signed provenance manifest, following a public open standard, that records which app produced the asset, the actions taken on it (for example crop, resize, colour adjustment, or a generative fill), and the ingredients it was made from (other assets, each of which may carry its own manifest). The manifest is bound to the asset by a hash of its bytes and signed with the issuing app's certificate; it can be embedded in the file, stored in a cloud and looked up later, or both. Creators choose whether to include their identity. About {{exports_per_day}} exports a day carry credentials, about {{generative_share}} of them record a generative step, and a composite can have up to {{max_ingredients}} ingredients. A public inspection tool receives about {{verifications_per_day}} requests a day: someone drops in a file, and the tool reports what credentials it found and whether they validate. Content credentials describe history and who claims to have made an asset; under this exercise's framing they are never a guarantee that the asset depicts something true.
sections.problem: Design the data model for manifests and their analysis. Cover: manifests (id, the asset hash they are bound to, the issuing app and version, signer certificate, signing time, whether creator identity was included), recorded actions as rows with their order and kind (including generative steps, recorded without their prompts), ingredient relations between manifests as a graph, where each manifest is stored (embedded, cloud, both); and verification results as observations: which file was checked, when, against which trust list version, and with which outcome (valid, signature invalid, signer not trusted, asset changed since signing, no credentials found, credentials recovered from the cloud). Then show how to answer "every asset derived, directly or through ingredients, from asset X", "share of exports with a generative step by app and month", and "outcomes of inspections by outcome and week", and say what analytics must never hold.
sections.constraints: A signed manifest never changes; an edit creates a new manifest that lists the previous one as an ingredient. Verification outcomes are reproducible: the same file checked against the same trust list version gives the same outcome. No image content, prompt text or uploaded file is kept for analytics; inspected files are hashed and discarded. Creator identity appears in analytics only as a flag saying it was included, never the identity itself.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and limits are hypothetical. The trust list (which signers are recognised) changes a few times a year. A file can carry no manifest, one manifest, or a chain of them. Hash functions are fixed per manifest version. Rules here are this exercise's rules; check current docs for the open standard's details.
sections.criteria: Immutable manifests bound by hash and signed, with edits as new manifests that list ingredients; actions as ordered rows, generative steps recorded without prompts; ingredients as a DAG with a lineage strategy (closure table or bounded recursion) and its maintenance cost; storage location as data; verification as append-only observations with the trust list version and precise outcome categories; "valid" never described as authenticity; identity reduced to a flag in analytics; each incident traced, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does "valid" mean the image is authentic?
clarifications.a: No. It means the manifest is intact, bound to these bytes, and signed by a signer on the trust list in force. Your report wording must say that.

clarifications.q: Can two manifests share an ingredient?
clarifications.a: Yes. The same stock photo can be an ingredient of thousands of composites, and an asset can be used twice in one composite.

clarifications.q: What happens when a site strips metadata on upload?
clarifications.a: The embedded manifest is gone. If a cloud copy exists, the tool may recover it by looking up the asset, which is a different outcome from "found embedded".

clarifications.q: Are prompts recorded?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. A generative action records which feature and model family were used, never the prompt.

clarifications.q: Can a manifest be revoked?
clarifications.a: A signer's certificate can be removed from the trust list. Earlier results are not rewritten; new checks give a new outcome.

hints: Manifests are nodes and ingredient relations are edges of a directed acyclic graph; because each manifest is bound to a hash of its own bytes and signed, a cycle cannot form.
Keep verification as an append-only observation with the trust list version it used. "Current status" of an asset is a derived view, not an updated column.
Lineage queries over a deep, wide graph need a closure table or bounded recursion; decide which and how it is maintained as new manifests arrive.
followups: Write the recursive query for "every asset derived from asset X" and say how you bound it when one ingredient is shared by millions of composites.
The trust list removes a signer. What happens to yesterday's results, to today's dashboard, and to the share of "valid" inspections by week?
An inspected file has no embedded manifest but the cloud has one for the same hash. How do you record that, and how does the weekly outcome mix change?
With up to {{max_ingredients}} ingredients per composite and {{exports_per_day}} exports a day, estimate edges per day. Would you maintain a closure table, and at what cost?
A creator turns off identity for future exports. What changes in your model for past manifests, and what can analytics still report?

rules.ask: The trust list changed yesterday. Is your flag the outcome then or now, and how do you reproduce last month's report?
What exactly does a valid result establish, and what would you write on the report so nobody reads more into it?
One stock image is an ingredient of 40 million composites. What does your lineage query do from that node, and how do you bound it?
Where would a prompt end up in your model, and how do you make sure it never does?
You stored the manifest as a document. How do you count generative steps by app and month without parsing every blob each time?

incidents: A trust list update removed one signer certificate. The "valid" share of inspections fell from 92% to 61% overnight, and a dashboard that recomputed every past result against the new list rewrote three months of history.

A popular site began stripping embedded metadata on upload. Inspections of files re-downloaded from it report "no credentials found", and a weekly report reads that as exports missing credentials, although about {{generative_share}} of those exports recorded a generative step at export time.

A template composite reused one stock asset as {{max_ingredients}} ingredients, and creators re-exported it thousands of times a day. The nightly closure-table job ran for nine hours and the lineage view fell a day behind.

templates.title: Shared libraries linked into documents — elements, versions, links and update propagation
templates.subtopic: versioned shared elements, link placements, reverse index, staleness and propagation

sections.scenario: Designers and brand teams keep shared libraries of colours, character and paragraph styles, logos and graphics: about {{libraries}} libraries, some shared with {{library_members}} members as viewers or editors. An element placed from a library into a document can be linked: when someone edits the element in the library, every document holding a linked placement should show the new version. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), an open document picks up the change within {{propagation_minutes}} minutes and a closed one picks it up when next opened, and a user can choose to keep the old version in one document by unlinking that placement, which then becomes an embedded copy. A brand's primary colour or logo can be linked into {{linked_documents}} documents. Brand teams ask: "if I change this colour, which documents change, and who owns them?", "how many documents still show the old logo?", and "how long do updates take to arrive?".
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: libraries, membership and roles over time; elements and their immutable versions (an edit, a rename, a delete, a restore); placements: which document version holds which element, at which element version, linked or embedded; the reverse index from an element to the documents that link it, and how it stays correct when documents are edited offline; propagation as events (update published, document notified, document applied) so that staleness and latency are measurable; and what happens when an element is deleted or a member loses access to the library. Then define "out of date" precisely and show the facts that answer the three questions above.
sections.constraints: Element versions never change once published. Edits to an element apply to linked placements in version order: a document never moves from a newer element version to an older one. A document keeps rendering even if the element is deleted or the user loses access (the document holds its last applied version). Document contents beyond placement ids and element ids never enter analytics. A brand team sees only documents shared with them, plus counts of the rest.
sections.assumptions: Library counts, member counts, fan-outs and propagation targets are hypothetical. A document can hold many placements of the same element. Document versions are recorded when saved; placements are read from each saved version's metadata. Devices can be offline for days.
sections.criteria: Immutable element versions with monotonic numbering by the library; placements at document-version grain with linked or embedded state and the applied element version; a reverse index derived from placements and robust to late offline saves; propagation as events with measurable latency and a stated population; a precise out-of-date definition separating pending, blocked and kept; membership over time and behaviour on loss of access or deletion; facts and access scoped to the brand team; each incident traced, contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is an edit that is reverted a new version?
clarifications.a: Yes. Reverting creates a new version with the old values; version numbers only go up.

clarifications.q: What does a document hold when its owner loses access to the library?
clarifications.a: The last version it applied, now unable to update. Report it apart from documents that simply have not opened yet.

clarifications.q: Can an element move between libraries?
clarifications.a: Yes, by copy: the copy is a new element with a record of where it came from.

clarifications.q: Does "out of date" count closed documents?
clarifications.a: That is your definition to make. Say which documents count, and over what period.

clarifications.q: Who is the owner shown to a brand team?
clarifications.a: Only owners of documents shared with that team; other documents appear as counts.

hints: Keep the placement at document-version grain: (document, document version, placement id, element id, element version applied, linked or embedded). The latest document version gives the current state; earlier ones give history.
The reverse index (element → documents) is derived from placements, keyed by element, and updated when document versions arrive, including late ones from offline devices.

Out of date = linked placement whose applied element version is below the element's latest published version; separate "pending" (not opened since the edit), "blocked" (no access) and "kept" (unlinked by choice).
followups: Write the query for "documents still showing the old logo" with its three categories, and say how many rows it reads at {{linked_documents}} linked documents.
The colour is edited and reverted within two minutes. Show the events and the applied versions for an open document and for a closed one.
Define propagation latency for an open document with a {{propagation_minutes}}-minute target. Which timestamps do you use, and which documents are excluded from the percentile?
An element is deleted while linked into thousands of documents. What does each placement row say afterwards, and what does the brand team see?
A designer edits offline for three days and links the logo into a new document. When does the reverse index learn about it, and what did "which documents change" answer meanwhile?

rules.ask: The primary colour is linked into many thousands of documents. What happens to that one row on every save, and how do you answer which ones are out of date?
Two updates to the same colour arrive at a document out of order. Which one does it keep, and how does your model prevent going backwards?
Is the version number assigned by the library or by the client that edited it? What happens when two editors save at once?
Is an unlinked placement out of date? How does your report tell "kept on purpose" from "never updated"?
A member leaves the library. What happens to the placements in their documents, and how do they show up in the counts?

incidents: A brand colour was edited and reverted within a minute. Documents applied the two updates in different orders, and about a fifth of the {{linked_documents}} linked documents ended on the edited colour that had been reverted.

A team library was unshared from a departing agency's {{library_members}} members. Their documents can no longer update, and the "out of date" count for the logo climbs every week with documents nobody can fix.

Propagation latency p95 is reported as 3 minutes against a {{propagation_minutes}}-minute target, but it only measures documents that were open; documents opened days later are missing from the percentile, and brand teams see old logos in shared files.

templates.title: Agreements waiting on a signer — the current step, the holder after delegations, and hours waited
templates.subtopic: as-of state from events, delegation chains (recursive CTE), sequential steps, waits

sections.scenario: An e-signature service's customers want an administrator report of agreements stuck waiting on someone. The extract you are given holds only metadata and events, never document contents: agreements (one row per agreement, with signing_order 'sequential' or 'parallel', sent_at NULL for a draft, optional expires_at and cancelled_at, and status as it was when the extract was taken at {{extracted_at}}), agreement_participants (one row per participant named in the agreement, with a step number and a role), and agreement_events (viewed, reminded, delegated with delegate_to, signed, declined). Participants are pseudonymous ids. A sequential agreement goes step by step: a step's signers act only once every signer at lower steps has signed. The extract has {{agreements}} agreements and {{events}} events.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, as of {{as_of}}, one row per signer that an open sequential agreement is waiting on: agreement_id, current_step, assigned_to, pending_with, hours_waiting, ordered by hours_waiting descending, then agreement_id, then assigned_to. An agreement is open at the as-of time when its signing_order is 'sequential', it was sent at or before that time, it was not cancelled at or before it, nobody declined at or before it, it has not expired, and at least one of its signers has not signed by then. Each signer row is a slot. The participant holding a slot can pass it on with a delegated event naming delegate_to; a delegate can delegate again, so follow the chain, counting only delegations at or before the as-of time.
