A slot is signed when its holder has a signed event at or before the as-of time. current_step is the lowest step with an unsigned signer slot; return a row for every unsigned signer slot at that step, with assigned_to the participant named in the slot and pending_with its holder at the as-of time. hours_waiting is the time from the moment the agreement reached the current step (the latest signature at any lower step, or sent_at if no lower step names a signer) to the as-of time, in hours rounded to 2 decimals. Delegating does not restart the wait, and viewed and reminded events change nothing. {{level_rules}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Boundaries are inclusive (a signature, delegation, decline or cancellation at exactly the as-of time has happened), except expiry. Do not use status: it describes the agreement at extraction, after the as-of time. In production the event table holds billions of rows across many customers.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, ids and times, all in UTC. Participant ids are unique within an agreement, delegates included; a holder delegates at most once; a delegate's id never appears in agreement_participants. Only a slot's holder signs or declines it. No contents, field values, names or email addresses are in the extract.
sections.criteria: State rebuilt from events up to the as-of time, never from the status column; open agreements filtered by sent, cancelled, declined and expiry with exact boundaries; delegation chains followed (recursive CTE) only up to the as-of time; slots signed by any holder in the chain; current step as the lowest unsigned signer step and the wait from the latest lower signature or sent_at; cc rows and parallel agreements excluded; deterministic ordering; can explain snapshots, chain materialisation and grouped orders.

clarifications.q: Can I filter on status = 'in_progress'?
clarifications.a: No. It is the status at extraction; an agreement completed or cancelled since the as-of time was still waiting then.

clarifications.q: Does a delegation reset the wait?
clarifications.a: No. The wait is the agreement's wait at that step, measured from when it reached the step.

clarifications.q: If step 1 is signed exactly at the as-of time, which step is current?
clarifications.a: The next signer step, with 0 hours waited.

clarifications.q: Who is pending_with if a delegation happens after the as-of time?
clarifications.a: The holder at the as-of time, so the delegation is ignored.

clarifications.q: Should parallel agreements appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only sequential agreements wait on one step at a time.

hints: Build the state from events filtered to the as-of time first, then decide which agreements are open.

A recursive CTE starting at each signer slot and joining delegated events on the current holder walks the chain; the last holder is pending_with, and a signed event by any holder in the chain completes the slot.
The current step is a MIN over unsigned slots; the time it was reached is a MAX over the signatures at lower steps, falling back to sent_at.
followups: Why can't step = current_step - 1 find the moment the current step was reached? Give a case from the data.
Turn this into a daily snapshot table of waiting slots for the last 90 days. What is its grain, and how is it rebuilt when late events arrive?
At billions of events, how would you avoid walking delegation chains from scratch for every report?
An administrator wants the same report for agreements with groups whose members act in any order inside each group. What changes in the query?

rules.ask: The status column was written when the extract was taken, two weeks after the as-of time. Which agreements does that filter drop, and were they waiting at the as-of time?
What stops your recursion, and what would happen if the data contained a delegation cycle?
The step before the current one names only cc rows, or the numbering skips. Where does your wait start then?
Does handing the slot to someone else change how long the agreement has waited? What would the sender expect to see?
An event at exactly the as-of time: has it happened? Show the comparison you wrote.

incidents: A customer's report, built on the extract's status column, showed no stalled agreements for a week that had dozens; every one of them was completed by the time the extract ran at {{extracted_at}}.
After a bulk delegation tool reassigned thousands of slots twice in a row, a report that followed only one hop sent reminders to people who no longer held the slot.

templates.title: Creative app usage analytics that honour opt-outs and compare fairly across versions
templates.subtopic: event contracts, sessions, opt-out deletion, cross-version metrics

sections.scenario: A suite of {{apps}} creative apps for desktop and mobile is used by about {{monthly_users}} people a month. Each app can send usage events: launch, session heartbeats, feature used (a tool invoked, a panel opened, an export, a save to cloud documents), errors and quit. Desktop apps are updated on the user's schedule, so {{versions_live}} versions of a popular app are in use at once, and a desktop app that is offline buffers its events for up to {{offline_days}} days before sending them. Users can turn off usage-data sharing in their settings at any time. Product teams want weekly active users per app and feature, feature adoption by version, session length, and the share of new users who reach a first export, and they want each release compared fairly with the one before it.
sections.problem: Design the usage analytics platform: the event contract and how it is versioned; collection from the apps (batching, offline buffering, retries); honouring the sharing setting end to end; sessionisation; a canonical feature catalogue so metrics compare across versions; storage layers and serving; and data-quality monitoring per release. Define a weekly active user and a session precisely.
sections.constraints: Under this exercise's rule (check current docs for the real products), when a user turns sharing off the apps stop sending from that moment, and identifiable event rows already received for that user are removed from every store within {{delete_days}} days; aggregates that no longer identify anyone may stay. No document content, file names or text typed in the apps ever enters an event. Dashboards refresh daily; a release-comparison view must be available within 6 hours of a release's first events. Events arrive late, out of order and sometimes twice.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and service levels are hypothetical. Each event carries an app id, app version, platform, an install id (random per installation), a pseudonymous user id, the client's event time, a per-install sequence number and an event id. The account's privacy settings service publishes an event, with the pseudonymous user id and the time, whenever the sharing setting changes.
sections.criteria: A typed, versioned event contract with no content fields; precise definitions of active users (suite and per app, with background launches excluded) and sessions that do not depend on one version's heartbeat; a canonical feature catalogue mapping per-version event names, enforced before release; event-time attribution with dedup on event id and a stated finality window for late offline uploads; the sharing setting enforced at collection and as tracked deletion across raw, derived and backup stores within the deadline; release comparison that controls for who updates early; per-release data-quality checks (unmapped events, volume shifts, opted-out senders); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a user who opens two apps on the same day one active user or two?
clarifications.a: One for the suite, and one in each app's own count. Say which number you report where.

clarifications.q: What counts as active: a launch, or doing something?
clarifications.a: You define it. Product is unhappy that an app launched by a background updater counts today.

clarifications.q: Do feature names stay the same across versions?
clarifications.a: No. Tools are renamed, split and merged in redesigns, and each app team names its own events.

clarifications.q: How long is raw data kept?
clarifications.a: You propose it; identifiable rows are always subject to the deletion rule.

clarifications.q: Can the apps send anything when sharing is off?
clarifications.a: Nothing about usage. The settings change itself reaches you through the privacy settings service.

hints: Write down what one weekly active user and one session are before choosing stores; both depend on fields in the event contract.
A feature's identity must outlive its event name: map (app, version, event name) to a canonical feature id in a versioned catalogue owned with the app teams.
The sharing setting has two jobs: stop collection, and remove what is identifiable. List every place a user's rows live, including derived tables and backups.
followups: Define a session for a desktop app that stays open for eight hours while the user works in bursts, and for a phone app sent to the background every few minutes.
A redesign splits one tool into two. How does "adoption of the tool" compare between the old version and the new one?
A desktop app sends {{offline_days}} days of buffered events at once. Which days' numbers change, and when are they final?
A user turns sharing off. Walk through every table their data lives in and what happens to each within {{delete_days}} days.
Users who update in the first week differ from those who wait. How do you compare a release with the previous one fairly?

rules.ask: One person uses three installations of the app on two computers and a tablet. How many weekly active users is that in your design, and is that the number product wants?
A new version changes the heartbeat interval. How do you keep session counts comparable between versions?
The user's rows also fed yesterday's aggregates and a feature-adoption table keyed by user. Which of those must change, and which may stay?
Who owns the mapping from event names to features, and what stops a release from shipping an unmapped event?
A desktop app was offline for {{offline_days}} days. Which day do its events count on, and what does that do to yesterday's dashboard?

incidents: A release of one app renames the event for its most-used tool. As the new version rolls out, the dashboard shows that tool's weekly use falling 40% while nothing changed for users.
One mobile app version keeps sending usage events for 9 days after users turn sharing off, from about 2% of that app's users.
A new desktop version sends its heartbeat every 15 minutes instead of every 5; average sessions per user for that version fall by a third, and a team reads it as the redesign hurting engagement.

After a network outage at a large customer site, thousands of desktop apps upload up to {{offline_days}} days of buffered events in one hour; a daily active-user chart grouped by arrival date shows a one-day spike of 6%.

templates.title: Generative image service analytics with credits, moderation and content credentials, prompts never kept
templates.subtopic: request lifecycle, credit reconciliation, privacy by construction, percentiles

sections.scenario: Generative image features are offered in {{surfaces}} surfaces: desktop apps, mobile apps and the web. About {{requests}} generation requests arrive a day. Each request names a feature (an image from a text description, filling a selected area, extending the canvas), one of the {{model_versions}} model versions being served, the surface and the account. A request can be rejected by input moderation, succeed with several variants, fail, time out or be cancelled by the user; output moderation can block some or all of the variants. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), each plan includes a monthly allowance of generative credits, a successful request consumes credits according to the feature, and failed, blocked or cancelled requests consume none. Every image the service returns carries content credentials: provenance metadata recording that a generative tool made it. Product, trust-and-safety, finance and support teams all want analytics on this service.
sections.problem: Design the analytics platform: the events the service emits for a request's lifecycle; how prompts and images are kept out; the metrics (success rate, latency percentiles per model version and surface, moderation outcomes by stage and category, credits consumed per account against its allowance, and content-credentials coverage); reconciliation with the credit ledger that enforces allowances; and serving with dashboards no more than {{freshness}} behind.
sections.constraints: Prompts, uploaded reference images, selections and generated images never enter analytics, logs or the warehouse, and nothing derived from a prompt's text does either. Moderation categories are reported only in aggregates of at least {{min_count}} requests. Credits per account per month in analytics must equal the credit ledger exactly. Latency percentiles must be correct across hosts and regions.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and thresholds are hypothetical. The credit ledger is a separate service and the authority for entitlement; analytics reads its events. Clients may retry a request that timed out; a retry carries the original request id only if the client kept it.
sections.criteria: Content kept out by construction (allowlisted typed schema, no free text, enforcement at the producer and a scanner as a backstop, a purge path when it fails); a request lifecycle keyed by request id so retries, partial output blocks and charges count once; precise definitions of success and moderation rates; credits reconciled to the ledger, which stays the authority, with corrections flowing through; mergeable latency sketches per model version and surface, with client and server latency kept apart; moderation categories only above the minimum count; coverage of content credentials measured at the point of return and on export separately; fair comparison of versions (one change at a time, or a holdout); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does analytics need the prompt for quality analysis?
clarifications.a: No. Prompt-level research is out of scope and has its own controls; this platform never receives prompts.

clarifications.q: Is a request with four variants, one blocked by output moderation, a success?
clarifications.a: The user receives three images and is charged under this exercise's rule. You define how it counts in success rate and in moderation rate.

clarifications.q: Which latency matters?
clarifications.a: Product wants time from request to first image shown and to all variants; the service measures its own server time. Say what you measure where.

clarifications.q: Who owns the credit numbers?
clarifications.a: The credit ledger. Analytics must agree with it, not replace it.

clarifications.q: Who attaches content credentials?
clarifications.a: The service, when it returns an image. Some export paths in apps can lose them later; you decide what "coverage" measures.

hints: Keep content out by construction: an allowlisted event schema with typed fields and no free text, enforced where events are produced, not by a filter downstream.
One request, many events: give the request an id and model its lifecycle as states, so retries, partial blocks and charges are each counted once.
Percentiles do not average; keep mergeable sketches per model version, surface and time bucket.
followups: Walk through one request that returns four variants, one blocked by output moderation: which events are emitted, and how is it counted in success, moderation and credits?
How do you show a privacy reviewer that no prompt text can reach the warehouse, including through error messages and logs?
Credits in analytics differ from the ledger for 0.3% of accounts. How do you find out why?
A new model version ships to one surface. How do you compare its latency and moderation rates with the old version fairly?
Trust-and-safety asks for moderation block rates per category, per country, per day. What do you give them, given the {{min_count}} rule?

rules.ask: Where exactly is the prompt dropped in your design, and what stops a developer adding it to an error field next quarter?
Two regions each report their own p95. How do you get the global p95 for one model version?
A client retries a timed-out request without the original id, and both attempts succeed. How many credits does the account lose, and what does analytics show?
Credit totals must equal the ledger exactly. Which metrics may you sample, and which must count every request?
The ledger is corrected after a support refund. How does the correction reach last month's dashboards?

incidents: An app release starts putting the prompt text into a free-text error detail on failed requests; it reaches the raw event store for 3 days before anyone notices.
For one month, credits shown in analytics exceed the credit ledger by 4%: timed-out requests retried by clients were logged as separate charged generations.
A new model version and a new moderation threshold ship on the same day on one of the {{surfaces}} surfaces; output-moderation blocks rise from 1.5% to 6%, and product asks which change caused it.
Content-credentials coverage for one output format falls to 70% after a service release, and the dashboard cannot say whether the credentials were never attached or the metric stopped seeing them.

templates.title: Document and e-signature services: usage reporting and audit trails without reading contents
templates.subtopic: audit trails, billable usage, data residency, content exclusion

sections.scenario: A document platform offers PDF services through an API and through apps (convert to PDF, export to other formats, recognise text in scans, compress, combine, protect) and e-signature agreements: a sender creates an agreement, participants receive it, view it, sign, delegate or decline, and it completes, expires or is cancelled. About {{customers}} enterprise customers use it, producing about {{operations}} document operations and agreement events a day, stored in {{regions}} regions; each customer's data stays in the region it chose. Customers want three things: usage reports (operations by type, pages processed, and transactions consumed against their contract), an audit trail for each agreement that they can download and show to an auditor, and admin reports (who sent what, completion times, agreements waiting on a signer).
sections.problem: Design event collection from the document and e-signature services, the per-customer reporting store, the audit trail (completeness, ordering, tamper evidence and retention), data residency, and how you guarantee that contents are never read. Say what "complete" means for an audit trail, and how a customer can trust the usage numbers they are invoiced on.
sections.constraints: Document contents, page text, file names and form-field values never enter the event pipeline, reports or logs; events carry only ids, types, statuses, timestamps, page counts and sizes. Audit trails are kept for {{retention_years}} years and must show events in their true order, with nothing missing or altered. The usage numbers in a customer's report must equal the numbers on their invoice. No customer can ever see another customer's events.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and periods are hypothetical. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), an agreement's final audit report is produced when it reaches a terminal status, with times in UTC. Participants' names and email addresses appear in the agreement's own audit trail, which belongs to the customer, but never in usage analytics.
sections.criteria: Separates the per-agreement audit trail from per-customer usage analytics; content excluded by typed schemas with no free text, checked at the producer and scanned downstream, with a purge path; billable operations keyed by operation id so retries count once, and one usage table feeding both report and invoice; audit events ordered by a sequence assigned by the agreement's owning service (not by arrival), completeness checked against the agreement's state machine before a final report is issued; tamper evidence (per-agreement hash chain anchored in an append-only, separately controlled store) and retention for the stated years; in-region storage with only non-identifying aggregates leaving a region; tenant isolation enforced in the data-access layer; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can we keep file names to help support?
clarifications.a: No. Treat file names as content; give support an id they can look up together with the customer.

clarifications.q: Who counts pages: the converter or the billing system?
clarifications.a: You decide; the customer's report and their invoice must agree.

clarifications.q: Is a failed conversion billed?
clarifications.a: Not under this exercise's rule. A retried conversion of the same request is billed once if it succeeds.

clarifications.q: How is an audit trail used?
clarifications.a: Customers download it as evidence of who did what and when; it must hold up for years.

clarifications.q: Do one agreement's events ever come from more than one region?
clarifications.a: Participants act from anywhere, but each agreement belongs to its customer's region; events can reach that region late or out of order.

hints: There are two products here: an audit trail per agreement (complete, ordered, tamper-evident, long-lived) and usage analytics per customer (aggregated, billable). They need different stores and guarantees.
Keep contents out by construction: typed event schemas with no free-text fields, validated where events are produced.
Give every billable operation an id so retries count once, and derive both the invoice and the usage report from the same table.
followups: What does one agreement's audit trail look like as data, and what makes it tamper-evident?
How do you make sure the usage report and the invoice can never disagree?
A participant's "viewed" event arrives after their "signed" event. What does the audit trail show?
How do you meet residency in {{regions}} regions and still give the platform team a global usage dashboard?
A customer's auditor asks you to prove an audit trail has not been altered in {{retention_years}} years. What do you show?

rules.ask: The chain is computed per agreement. What stops someone with database access from rewriting the whole chain?
A converter's debug log line includes a snippet of extracted text. Where does that line end up in your design, and how would you know?
Two events for one agreement arrive in the wrong order through different regions. Whose clock decides their order in the audit trail?
Which customer data leaves its region to feed that global view, and is it allowed to?
A conversion times out on the client and is retried, and both attempts finish. How many pages does the customer pay for?

incidents: A conversion worker release logs the first 200 characters of recognised text in a debug field; the field flows into the per-customer reporting pipeline for 2 days.
A customer disputes a monthly usage report showing 12% more pages than their own records: retried conversions that both completed were counted twice.
0.3% of audit trails show "signed" before "viewed" because events relayed between regions were ordered by arrival time.
The event pipeline in one of the {{regions}} regions is down for 6 hours while signing keeps working; audit trails downloaded for agreements completed in that window are missing events.

templates.title: Cloud document storage and sync across devices, with conflicts, quotas and honest sync latency
templates.subtopic: content-addressed versions, conflicts, quota accounting, latency measurement

sections.scenario: Creative apps on desktop, tablet and phone save documents to cloud storage for about {{users}} users. A cloud document is a set of components (layers, artboards, embedded images, references to fonts) described by a manifest, and documents reach {{largest_doc}}. A typical user edits on {{devices}} devices, sometimes offline, with autosave every few minutes and named versions saved by hand. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), each plan has a storage quota ({{quota}} in this scenario), version history is kept for 30 days and does not count toward the quota, and deleted documents count until the trash is emptied. A save on one device should be visible on the user's other online devices within {{sync_target}} at p95.
sections.problem: Design storage and sync: the document and version model; uploading large documents by sending only changed components; making a version's commit atomic; propagating it to the other devices; handling conflicts when two devices edit the same document; quota accounting and enforcement; and measuring sync latency honestly.
sections.constraints: A saved edit is never lost, even when two devices conflict. A version becomes visible only when all of its components are stored. Uploads over poor mobile networks must resume rather than restart. Quota is checked when a save is accepted; a user over quota can still open, download and export everything. Storage cost matters: most edits change a small part of a large document.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, sizes and targets are hypothetical. Components can be addressed by a hash of their bytes. The apps cannot merge two pixel edits to the same layer automatically, but they can show two versions side by side.
sections.criteria: Content-addressed components with resumable, chunked uploads that send only what changed; a version committed by a conditional write of its manifest only after the server verifies every component exists; a version graph with parent pointers, conflicts detected as siblings (never by device clocks) and both kept, with a clear rule for what each device shows; quota computed from the logical size of current documents and trash under the stated rule, checked before upload begins; garbage collection by reachability from live versions with a grace period; end-to-end sync latency measured from commit to the other device's acknowledgement, including devices that were offline, reported separately from online-device latency; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can two devices edit the same document at once?
clarifications.a: Yes, though usually it is one person moving between devices, sometimes offline. Real-time co-editing is out of scope.

clarifications.q: Do identical components in two documents count twice toward the quota?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule the quota counts the logical size of each current document, so yes; deduplicated storage is your saving, not the user's.

clarifications.q: What does "visible" mean for sync latency?
clarifications.a: The other device shows the new version as current. You decide whether that requires the bytes to be downloaded.

clarifications.q: What happens when a user goes over quota?
clarifications.a: New cloud saves are refused with a clear message; nothing already stored is deleted.

hints: Separate immutable content (components addressed by hash) from the small, mutable pointer to the current version. A version commits by writing its manifest after all its components exist.
A conflict is two versions with the same parent. Keep both, then decide what each device shows.
Measure sync latency from the saving device's commit to the other device's acknowledgement, and include the devices you would rather not count.
followups: Walk through saving a {{largest_doc}} document in which one layer changed, over a connection that drops halfway.
Two devices edited the same document offline for a day. What does each device show when it reconnects, and what is stored?
How do you account for quota when components are shared between versions and between documents?
Version history is kept for 30 days. How do you delete expired components without deleting one that a current version still uses?
Your sync latency p95 meets {{sync_target}}, but users say sync takes minutes. What are you not measuring?

rules.ask: A device's clock is two hours behind. Whose edits win under your rule, and does the user lose work?
A component is shared by 40 versions across three documents and one document is deleted. When is the component removed, and what proves nothing still needs it?
The other device is a laptop that was asleep for three days. How does it catch up, and does that count in your latency metric?
These documents are layered images, not text. What can be merged automatically, and what cannot?
A user goes over quota while an autosave is uploading. Do you refuse the save after half of it has been uploaded?

incidents: After a client release, devices on unstable networks sometimes publish a manifest before all of its components are uploaded; other devices open that version with missing layers.
A user edits the same document offline on two devices for a day. On reconnecting, one device's edits vanish from the current version because the device with the later clock won.
A storage backfill recomputes usage and includes version history by mistake; 3% of users appear to be over their {{quota}} quota, and their saves are refused.
The sync latency dashboard shows p95 under {{sync_target}} while support tickets say sync takes minutes: the metric stops at the server commit and leaves out devices that were asleep.

templates.title: Restating web analytics history after a customer changes processing rules or classifications
templates.subtopic: versioned rules, lookup joins, atomic switch-over, tenant isolation

sections.scenario: A web analytics product collects hits from customers' sites and apps (page views, link clicks and custom events), about {{hits}} a day across all customers. One large customer has {{sites}} sites reporting into its account and keeps {{history_months}} months of history. Two kinds of customer configuration change what reports show. Processing rules, set by the customer, act on each hit as it is processed: copy a query-string parameter into a dimension, rename a page, assign a marketing channel. Classifications are lookup tables the customer uploads: tracking code to campaign, product code to category, page to site section. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), classifications apply to all history as soon as they are uploaded, while processing rules apply only to new hits unless the customer requests reprocessing of a date range, which must finish within {{deadline}}.
sections.problem: Design restatement: how raw and processed hits are stored; how classifications reach reports (joined at query time or materialised); how a reprocessing request replays history under the new rules; how reports switch from old numbers to new without mixing them; what happens to exports and scheduled reports already delivered; and how customers see what changed.
sections.constraints: Raw hits are immutable and kept for the history window. A report must never show a date range in which some days use the old rules and some the new, unless it says so. Reprocessing one customer must not slow other customers' current-day processing. Everything except the changed rule must stay as it was for each day (bot filtering, the report time zone, visit definitions), so totals the rule does not touch do not move. Daily data feeds delivered to customers' own storage may already contain the old values.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and periods are hypothetical. Each hit has a hit id, a site id and a received time; each customer account has a report time zone. Bot filtering is the product's own rule set, versioned separately from customer rules.
sections.criteria: Immutable raw hits with a processed layer versioned by rule set; classifications as versioned lookup tables joined at query time where affordable and materialised for heavy reports, with upload validation (normalisation, unmatched-key report) before they apply; reprocessing built beside the live version, per customer, with an atomic switch of the whole range and the old version kept for rollback; all other inputs (bot rules, time zone, visit logic) pinned per day, with an invariant check that untouched totals did not move; isolation through separate capacity or fair scheduling so one customer's replay cannot delay others; delivered feeds handled by versioned re-delivery and a change notice; a customer-visible change log; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a processing-rule change affect the past by default?
clarifications.a: Not under this exercise's rule; only a reprocessing request changes history.

clarifications.q: What about visits and visitors, not just hits?
clarifications.a: A rule could change which visit a hit belongs to only if it touched visit-defining fields; say whether you allow that.

clarifications.q: Can a customer undo a reprocessing?
clarifications.a: They can ask to. You decide what that costs.

clarifications.q: Is bot filtering part of the reprocessing?
clarifications.a: No. Reprocessing should apply the bot rules that were in force on each day.

clarifications.q: How big is one customer's history?
clarifications.a: Up to {{history_months}} months of that customer's hits, and the largest customers are a large share of all volume.

hints: Keep three layers: raw hits as received, processed hits under a versioned rule set, and reports. A restatement is a new version of the processed layer, built beside the old one.
A classification is a join against a lookup table. Decide which reports can join at query time and which need materialisation.
Pin everything except the changed rule to the version in force on each day, and check that totals the rule cannot affect did not move.
followups: A customer uploads a classification file. What do their reports show one minute later, and how?
Walk through a reprocessing request for {{history_months}} months: where it runs, how long it takes, how it is isolated from today's processing, and how reports switch over.
After reprocessing, total page views for the period change by 0.5%. Should they have? How do you find out why?
The customer's daily data feed already delivered the old values for those months. What do you do?
Two reprocessing requests from the same customer overlap in time and in date range. What happens?

rules.ask: Reprocessing fails halfway. What do reports show for the months already rewritten, and can you get the old numbers back?
A classification table has 40 million rows and a report scans a year of hits. What does the join cost, and when do you materialise?
Your reprocessing replays partition by partition. How do reports avoid showing some months new and some old in the meantime?
The largest customer's reprocessing would use a third of the cluster for a day. Who waits?
What exactly does the customer see that tells them their history changed, when and why?

incidents: A customer uploads a classification file in which 8% of tracking codes have a trailing space; across {{history_months}} months of reports, that share of campaign revenue moves to "unclassified".
A reprocessing job for one large customer runs past its {{deadline}} deadline; for 30 hours, half of the months show the new rules and half the old, and a quarterly report mixes them.

A processing-rule change that should only reassign marketing channels changes total page views for the reprocessed months by 0.5%: the replay used today's bot rules instead of the rules in force on each day.
The customer's warehouse, loaded from the daily data feed, now disagrees with the restated reports, and the customer's analysts ask which is right.

templates.title: An enterprise customer's audit request when your logs are incomplete
templates.subtopic: honesty under audit, evidence reconstruction, cross-team response

missing: administrator activity (who exported agreements and changed sharing settings)
document download events for agreements already completed
events from one region's integration API calls

sections.scenario: Your team owns the pipeline that records activity events for a document and e-signature service. An enterprise customer, {{customer}}, has asked for a complete activity report for the last six months as part of its own audit, due in {{deadline}} business days. While preparing it, your team finds that for {{gap}} four months ago the pipeline dropped {{missing}}. The agreements themselves and their signing audit trails are intact; the gap is in the activity log the customer asked for. Nobody outside your team knows yet, and the account team has already told the customer the report is "on track".
sections.problem: Tell me what you do in the first day, before the deadline, and afterwards. Cover how you establish exactly what is missing, what can honestly be reconstructed from other sources and how it is labelled, who must know and in what order, what the customer is told and by whom, and how you prevent the gap from recurring. Then tell me about a real time you had to tell a customer or stakeholder that data they relied on was incomplete, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own the customer relationship, the contract or legal advice. Nothing may be added to the report that did not happen or that cannot be traced to a source. The deadline can be discussed, but only through the account team.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Establishes the gap's extent with evidence (event types, period, customers affected, how measured) before describing it; escalates promptly to their manager, the account team, legal and security or privacy owners, especially given the "on track" message; never fabricates or silently backfills, and labels any reconstruction with source and limits; supports an honest customer message delivered by the owners, with a realistic date; checks and handles other affected customers; prevention with specific signals (per-type, per-hour completeness checks against source counts), owners and tests; real example with personal actions and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do other systems hold any of the missing activity?
clarifications.a: Partly: request logs at the service front door and storage access logs exist for some of the period, kept for different lengths of time and with less detail.

clarifications.q: Did any alert fire at the time?
clarifications.a: A volume alert existed, but its threshold was set for daily totals and the gap did not cross it.

clarifications.q: Do other customers have the same gap?
clarifications.a: Very likely; you have not checked yet.

clarifications.q: Does the customer's contract say anything about activity logs?
clarifications.a: You do not know. Legal and the account team do.

hints: Measure the gap before you describe it: which events, which period, which customers, and how you know.
Reconstructed evidence is still useful if it is labelled as reconstructed, with its source and its limits.
The account team's "on track" makes telling them sooner more important, not less.
followups: How do you establish the exact extent of the gap, and how sure can you be?
The front-door logs let you reconstruct part of the missing activity. How do you present it in the report so an auditor can rely on what it says and not on what it does not?
The account manager asks you to "fill the gap so the report looks complete". What do you say?
Other customers are affected too but have not asked. What should happen for them, and who decides?
In your real example, what did you personally say, to whom, and when?

rules.ask: Which events in your backfill can be traced to a source record, and how does the report tell those apart from events that were recorded at the time?
While legal reviews, the deadline approaches. What do you do in parallel, and what do you not do until they answer?
Who tells them, with which facts, and what is the first sentence?
The existing alert measured daily totals. What signal would have caught a gap of {{gap}} within an hour of it starting?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: A feature that works for most users but fails accessibility for some
templates.subtopic: launch decisions, accessibility as a requirement, process change

feature: a redesigned signing flow that completes in fewer steps
a new usage dashboard for customer administrators
a drag-and-drop report builder for web analytics customers
failure: screen-reader users cannot complete the main task
keyboard-only users cannot reach the main action
key information is shown by colour alone, with no text alternative
found_by: an accessibility review the week before launch
a customer's support ticket during the beta
an engineer on your team testing with assistive technology

sections.scenario: You lead the engineering work on {{feature}}. It tested well: most beta users finish their tasks faster than before, and the launch is in {{days}} days with marketing planned around it. Then {{found_by}} shows that {{failure}}. The old version, which the new one replaces, does not have this problem. The product manager wants to launch on time and fix the problem "in a follow-up".
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you size the problem and the fix, the options for the launch (and who decides), how users who depend on assistive technology are served whatever is decided, and what changes so the next feature does not reach this point with this problem. Then tell me about a real time you found a serious quality problem late, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You are not the product decision-maker. The fix is not trivial: your first estimate is two to three weeks. Some customers have accessibility requirements in their procurement terms; you do not know the details.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Treats accessibility as a requirement and the gap as a defect; sizes the fix quickly with the specialist and people who use assistive technology; lays out real options (delay, keep the old version available as an equal path, staged launch, scope change) with what each costs and who decides; refuses to estimate affected users by profiling assistive-technology use; makes sure an accessible path exists on launch day whatever is decided; brings in legal on customer terms without drawing legal conclusions; process change early in design and in the build (criteria in definition of done, automated checks plus manual testing with assistive technology); real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can the old version stay available?
clarifications.a: Technically yes, for a while; product would rather not run both.

clarifications.q: How many users are affected?
clarifications.a: You do not know. Usage analytics cannot tell you who uses assistive technology, and should not try to.

clarifications.q: Has the team built accessible interfaces before?
clarifications.a: Some engineers have; there is no checklist or automated check in the build.

clarifications.q: Who else should be involved?
clarifications.a: There is a central accessibility specialist who advises several teams, and legal can advise on customer terms.

hints: Treat it as a defect in a requirement, not as polish: the question is how users who cannot use the feature are served on launch day.
There are more than two options: delay, launch with the old version still available, launch to part of the audience, or change scope.
The process fix belongs before design and in the build, not only in a review before launch.
followups: How do you size the fix more precisely within a day, and who helps you?
The product manager says affected users are "a small percentage". How do you respond, and what data do you not try to collect?
Which launch option do you recommend, and what has to be true for it to be acceptable?
What changes in the team's process, and how would you know it worked on the next feature?
In your real example, what did you personally push for, and what was the outcome for the affected users?

rules.ask: What do users who rely on a screen reader or keyboard do between launch day and the follow-up, and who has committed to its date?
How would you know how many users are affected, and is "few" a reason that holds when the old version is being removed?
Marketing has already committed the date. What do you offer that keeps as much of the launch as possible?
Automated checks find some problems but not whether a task can be completed. What else goes into the process?
What did you personally recommend, and to whom?

templates.title: Adopting a technology the team does not know versus one it knows well
templates.subtopic: evaluation, reversibility, operational readiness, team capability

choice: a stream processor for the web analytics hit pipeline, instead of extending the hourly batch jobs the team knows
an open table format for the document-events lake, instead of the warehouse loads the team runs today
a workflow orchestrator new to the team, instead of its own scheduler for the stock ingestion jobs
champion: a new hire who ran it at a previous job
your manager, after a conference talk

sections.scenario: Your team of {{team}} engineers must deliver a large improvement within {{window}}. The proposal on the table is {{choice}}. It is championed by {{champion}}. The new option looks better on paper for this problem, but no one on the team except possibly its champion has run it in production, and the team is already on call for the existing pipelines.
sections.problem: How do you decide? Cover what evidence you gather and how, the criteria and who agrees them, how you reduce the risk of the option you choose, what it means for on-call and for the people on the team, and how the decision is recorded and revisited. Then tell me about a real time you chose between a familiar and an unfamiliar technology, and what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The delivery date does not move. No extra headcount this year. Whatever runs in production must have at least two people able to operate it at night.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Criteria agreed before comparison (fit to the requirement with numbers, operability, failure modes, team capability, cost, reversibility, hiring and support); a time-boxed spike on the real workload with written exit criteria; separates the merits from who champions it and handles the champion respectfully; risk reduction for the chosen option (incremental migration, parallel run, fallback path, at least two operators before on-call, runbooks); considers the people on the team (learning time, on-call fears) with concrete plans; a written decision record with revisit triggers and a switch-back signal; real example with outcome and personal judgement, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the familiar option good enough?
clarifications.a: It can probably meet the requirement with more work and more cost; it is not clear by how much.

clarifications.q: Is there company-wide guidance on the technology?
clarifications.a: No standard either way; another team uses it lightly.

clarifications.q: How does the team feel?
clarifications.a: Split. Some are excited to learn it; some worry about being paged for something they do not understand.

clarifications.q: Who makes the final decision?
clarifications.a: You, as the technical lead, with your manager's agreement.

hints: Write the criteria before you compare the options, and include running it at 3 a.m., not only building it.
A time-boxed spike with exit criteria turns opinions into evidence.
Ask what it costs to reverse the decision in six months, for each option.
followups: What is in your time-boxed evaluation, how long is it, and what result would make you choose the familiar option?
The champion is {{champion}}. How does that change how you run the evaluation and the conversation?
You choose the new technology. What has to be true before it takes production traffic and joins the on-call rota?
Halfway through the {{window}}, the new option is behind plan. What signals tell you to switch back, and who decides?
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you decide differently now?

rules.ask: What exact result from the spike would make you say no, and did you write it down before you started?
How long until two people can operate it at night, and what does on-call look like until then?
How do you tell the team member who is excited about it that the answer is no, if it is?
What does reversing it cost in six months, in engineer-weeks, and how did you estimate that?
What was your own position, and did it change?

templates.title: Mentoring an engineer moving from analytics into data engineering
templates.subtopic: skills assessment, stretch with safety, feedback, measurable progress

background: three years of SQL reports and dashboards for product teams
a strong analyst who built the team's most-used metric definitions
an analytics engineer who has only worked inside the warehouse
pipeline: the daily usage rollup for the document services
ingestion of stock contributor upload events
late-hit handling in the web analytics pipeline

sections.scenario: An engineer with {{background}} has moved into your data engineering team, and your manager asks you to mentor them. The goal is that in {{months}} months they own {{pipeline}}: they build changes to it, review others' changes, and take their share of on-call for it. They are confident with SQL and with what the numbers mean, and less so with version control workflows, testing, distributed processing, backfills and production operations. They are keen, and a little worried about being paged.
sections.problem: How do you approach it? Cover how you find out where they actually are, the plan and its milestones, how you choose their first pieces of work, how you give feedback, how you protect both them and the pipeline while they learn, and how you and they will know it has worked. Then tell me about a real time you helped someone grow into a new kind of role, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You keep your own delivery commitments; mentoring is part of your time, not all of it. The pipeline has paying customers downstream. The engineer's manager, not you, writes their performance review.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Finds the starting point through real work and conversation rather than a test; builds on their analytics strengths (tests, data checks, metric definitions) while closing specific gaps (version control, testing, distributed processing, idempotent backfills, operations); a written plan with observable milestones agreed together; first tasks real but recoverable, widening in scope; safety for the pipeline and the person (review, staged rollout, shadowed then reverse-shadowed on-call, runbooks); timely, specific, kind feedback, and an incident treated as learning; transparent coordination with their manager; adjusts the plan when progress is slow and distinguishes plan, support and fit; real example with personal actions and evidence of growth, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: What does the engineer want?
clarifications.a: To become a data engineer and stay one; they have said they would like to keep using their analytics strengths.

clarifications.q: Is there documentation for the pipeline?
clarifications.a: Some, out of date. Two people know it well, you and one other engineer.

clarifications.q: What does on-call involve?
clarifications.a: About one page a week, mostly late inputs and occasional backfills.

clarifications.q: Can you choose their first tasks?
clarifications.a: Yes, with the team lead's agreement.

hints: Start from their strengths: someone who knows what the numbers mean can write the tests and checks the pipeline lacks.
Choose work that is real but recoverable, and widen it as evidence grows.
Agree observable milestones together, so progress is visible to them, to you and to their manager.
followups: How do you find out what they already know and where the real gaps are, without making it an exam?
What are their first three pieces of work, and why in that order?
Their first production change causes a small incident. What do you do that day, and in the following week?
Halfway through, progress is slower than planned. How do you tell whether the plan, the support or the fit is the problem, and what do you say to them?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and how did you know it had worked?

rules.ask: When do you stop driving and let them drive, and how do you decide they are ready?
Your reviews of their code are long. How do you keep them useful without overwhelming them?
When does their first night on call happen, and what is in place so a page they cannot solve does not become a crisis?
Give me an example of feedback you would give in the first month, word for word.
What do you share with their manager, and do they know what you share?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for creative, document and marketing software
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, content exclusion, restatement and provenance

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: document and agreement contents never readable by the analytics that measures them
the same numbers in a customer's usage report, their invoice and their audit trail
history restated whenever a customer changes how their data is classified
provenance recorded for every asset the system produces or edits
scale: tens of millions of individual users
billions of events a day from customers' sites and apps

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change in creative, document and marketing software, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The creative, document and marketing setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example typed event schemas with no free text and producer-side enforcement; one billable table feeding report, invoice and audit; versioned processed data built beside the live version with an atomic switch; provenance records attached at each step with ingredients linked, described as metadata rather than proof of authenticity); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a document or analytics system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one record: where it enters, which fields it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A free-form field in your events could carry anything a client puts in it. How would you guarantee it never carries document contents?
When history is recomputed, what do readers see while it runs, and can you get the previous numbers back?
An asset is edited, exported to another format and combined with two others. What does its provenance record say, and what could make that record wrong?
